claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in HEAs is governed by the synergy between passive-film stability and alloy hardness.
An HEA combining a stable, self-healing passive film with high hardness will have superior resistance to combined wear-corrosion degradation.
Adjusting Cr or Al content can systematically alter passive-film stability.
Introducing solid-solution-strengthening elements can systematically alter alloy hardness.
The passive film acts as a protective barrier against corrosion.
A stable, self-healing passive film regenerates after mechanical damage and thereby maintains corrosion resistance.
High hardness reduces mechanical damage and consequently limits exposure of fresh alloy to the corrosive environment.
Alloys having both high passive-film stability and high hardness will show lower combined degradation rates than alloys lacking one or both properties.
The wear component will be lower in alloys having both high passive-film stability and high hardness.
The corrosion component will be lower in alloys having both high passive-film stability and high hardness.
The predicted relationship should hold where passive-film formation is possible and mechanical stresses do not exceed the alloy's yield strength.
The predicted relationship may fail where passive films cannot form or are rapidly dissolved.
The predicted relationship may fail under mechanical stresses that cause bulk material failure.
The relative contributions of passive-film stability and hardness may depend on the environment and alloy composition.
